key_takeaway: Lighter remains a strongly API-native, wallet-first venue: onboarding still starts from an Ethereum wallet and a credited deposit, not from an email or embedded-wallet path, but once the account_index exists the platform exposes a mature API-key, auth-token, and sub-account stack.

findings: The product docs still say users need an Ethereum wallet to register a main account.
The docs explicitly separate main accounts and sub-accounts.
Each account or sub-account may register up to 256 API keys.
The get-started guide tells developers to discover their account_index from an Ethereum address before initializing the signer.
It says API-key indices 0 and 1 are reserved for the web and mobile interfaces, while programmatic keys use 2-254.
Authenticated REST and websocket access is built around auth tokens generated from API private keys.
The docs now make the cold-start path explicit: to create a Lighter account, you simply deposit assets to Lighter.
Only after the deposit is credited does a master account_index get generated.
The docs then direct users to query account_index from contract or API and only afterward move on to API-key setup.
Ethereum mainnet deposits are contract-driven and require an L1 wallet.
The docs expose createIntentAddress as a pre-account deposit path for USDC from supported EVM chains via CCTP.
Fast withdrawals and transfers to other L1 addresses still require the wallet's Ethereum private key.
The docs describe a full API-key model with per-key public/private key pairs and per-key nonce management.
Canonical auth tokens can last up to 8 hours, and read-only auth tokens can last from 1 day to 10 years.
Generating API keys does not require the L1 private key, but associating them with the account still does.
The platform still separates Standard and Premium accounts.
Premium accounts are explicitly positioned for HFT and come with materially different sendTx/sendTxBatch limits and latency.
Standard accounts are limited to 60 REST requests per rolling minute.
Premium accounts use a weighted model and get a separate transaction bucket for sendTx and sendTxBatch.
The docs say limits apply at both IP and L1-address level, depending on endpoint type.
The docs still support multi-signature and smart-wallet usage, but note feature differences where Ethereum-private-key-dependent actions are unavailable.
Secure withdrawal remains available, while some flows such as transfers cannot be completed the same way.

signals: The visible UI still says Connect Wallet and Connect Wallet to Trade.
A lightweight HTML and text probe did not expose obvious email, social-login, or embedded-wallet vendor markers.

public_market_data.finding: Live market metadata is publicly accessible.

public_apikey_metadata.finding: The endpoint returned public API-key metadata such as api_key_index, nonce, public_key, and transaction_time for an existing account without an auth token.

findings: nextNonce returned nonce 0 for account_index 0 with api_key_index 2.
nextNonce also returned nonce 0 for a clearly arbitrary large account_index.
api_key_index 255 on nextNonce returned invalid api key index.

interpretation: Lighter still does not present as an email-first or embedded-wallet-first venue. The live app and current docs both reinforce a wallet-first posture.

The current docs make the cold-start path more explicit than a generic API-first reading would: deposit first, wait for crediting, then obtain account_index, then associate API keys, then generate auth tokens and trade.
The existence of createIntentAddress before account creation confirms that the deposit rail is available before the exchange account exists.

The live apikeys query shows that some API-key metadata is publicly queryable, but that does not reduce the real bootstrap friction because trading still requires account ownership, API-key association, and signer/auth-token generation.
nextNonce should still not be treated as a trustworthy onboarding signal, because public responses can look valid even when they do not prove that a usable trading account has been bootstrapped.

assessment.key_friction: A user still needs an Ethereum wallet, a credited deposit, a generated account_index, and L1-authorized API-key association before the mature API stack becomes usable.
